  • Check Manager Count before creating an administrator (1.4).
  • Disable the accounts of people who leave; a disabled account frees a seat.
  • Do not share admin or give UM to someone who only needs to read.
  • Review profiles after an organisational change.
  • Use Teams for cross-area work, not to duplicate users.
  • Document which profile each group has; the next administrator will thank you.

docs.text:

  • Companies and contacts (2.3).
  • Tickets and workflow (Part 03).

docs.title: Authentication and security
docs.text:
Authenticating is not filling in a form: it is proving who you are before the product lets you do anything. In Pandora ITSM that door can stay at home, be delegated to a directory or shared with Pandora FMS. Choosing the wrong method does not break the console on day one; it leaves it open or locks out someone who should be able to get in.

The point of this chapter is simple: authentication is configured once and reviewed every time the organisation changes. A directory that no longer exists, a password policy nobody remembers and a 2FA that depends on email are very effective ways of locking yourself out of your own tool.

docs.title: How you get into Pandora ITSM
docs.text:
Access has two layers that should not be mixed:

  • Authentication: who you are. The configured method resolves it.
  • Authorisation: what you can do. Groups and profiles in 2.1 resolve it.

A user can authenticate correctly and have no permissions at all. Or the other way around: have a huge profile and be unable to log in because their directory is down. The first layer is here; the second is in 2.1.

Super administrators are the exception: they always authenticate locally in Pandora ITSM, even if the rest of the users use AD, LDAP or Pandora FMS. It is a deliberate decision so that a directory failure does not leave the product without a master key.

docs.title: Authentication method
docs.text:
Configuration is in Setup → Setup → Authentication configuration.

Method What it uses When it makes sense Local Pandora ITSM Users and passwords in the database Small installations or no central directory LDAP Standard LDAP directory Organisations with OpenLDAP, 389 Directory Server, etc. Active Directory Microsoft AD Companies with accounts and groups in AD Pandora FMS API v2 of a PFMS server Environments that already centralise users in Pandora FMS

Pandora ITSM checks the configured remote method first. If the user exists and the password is correct, they get in; if it fails, they can use local authentication only if fallback is enabled.

docs.title: Local authentication
docs.text:
It is the default and the simplest option: users live in tusuario and the password is checked against the database.

  • Users are created and edited in People → User management (2.1).
  • The password policy applies here.
  • Password recovery sends an email link, so it needs working SMTP.
  • Super administrators always use this path.

For a small installation it is enough. For an organisation with a directory, duplicating users in two places usually ends up in orphan accounts.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Delegating to Microsoft Active Directory centralises accounts and credentials. Pandora ITSM still needs the profile and the group: AD says who you are; ITSM decides what you can do.

Connection fields:

Field What it means Active directory server Domain controller host or IP Active directory port Port, usually 389 or 636 Domain AD domain Start TLS Encrypts the connection with TLS

Important options:

  • Fallback to local authentication: if AD fails, allows login with the local password. Useful as a safety net; also a door to watch.
  • Advanced Configuration AD: links AD groups to Pandora ITSM profiles and groups. This is how an AD user inherits the right profile.
  • Automatically create remote users: creates the user in ITSM the first time they log in. You must choose level, profile, group and company; the blacklist (Automatically create blacklist) prevents certain accounts from being created on their own.
  • Test: checks the connection before saving. If it fails, the problem is usually DNS, TLS, domain or service credentials.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP is the generic equivalent of AD: a directory with users and groups. Pandora ITSM supports LDAPv1, LDAPv2 and LDAPv3.

Field What it means LDAP server LDAP host or IP LDAP port Port, usually 389 or 636 LDAP version LDAPv1, LDAPv2 or LDAPv3 Start TLS Encrypts the connection Base DN Starting point for the search Login attribute Attribute containing the user name (uid, sAMAccountName, etc.)

As with AD, there are Fallback to local authentication, Automatically create remote users and a blacklist. The Test button checks the connection.

Typical errors are a Base DN that is too high, a wrong login attribute or a TLS certificate that does not validate. If the bind fails, the user never even gets to check their password.

docs.title: Pandora FMS
docs.text:
Pandora ITSM can delegate authentication to a Pandora FMS server. It is useful when PFMS already centralises users and you do not want to maintain two directories.

  • URL to Pandora FMS setup: the full URL to API v2, for example https://<host>/pandora_console/api/v2.
  • Token: the API v2 token of the PFMS admin user.
  • Test: checks that the connection works before saving.

Automatic user creation lets you assign level, profile, group and company. Always choose least privilege; auto-creation with an administrator profile is an open door with a welcome sticker.

The remote user's password is managed on the PFMS server. If you change the password in ITSM, you are not changing the PFMS one.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text:
Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second proof after the password. Pandora ITSM integrates with Google Authenticator and compatible TOTP apps.

In Setup → Setup → Authentication configuration → Two-factor authentication:

  • Two-factor authentication: enables the feature.
  • Force 2FA for all users: requires users to configure it.
  • Warning 2FA for all users: only warns them that they should configure it.

Choose one of the two behaviour options before saving. If you neither force nor warn, 2FA is available but nobody notices.

Each user enables it in People → Edit my user:

  1. Enable Two-factor authentication.
  2. ITSM generates a key and a QR code (Pandora ITSM: <id-user> + key).
  3. Scan the QR or enter the key in the app.
  4. Enter the generated code and click Validate code.
  5. On the next login, after the password, it asks for the temporary code.

If a user loses the device, a super administrator can use Reset double factor authentication code. If the one who loses the device is the super administrator, the reset is done from their session: ITSM sends an email with a link valid for 15 minutes. That is why SMTP must work and the server clock must be in sync; a clock that is off invalidates the codes.

docs.title: Password policy
docs.text:
In Setup → Setup → Password policy setup. The policy does not apply to super administrators.

Option What it does Enable password policy Enables the rest of the rules Min. size password Minimum length; 5 by default Password must have numbers Requires at least one number Password must have symbols Requires at least one symbol Password expiration (days) Expiry; 0 means it never expires Force password change on first login Forces a change on login User blocked if login fails (minutes) Minutes of blocking after failed attempts Number of failed login attempts Attempts before blocking

If the policy is enabled, automatic password generation also respects it. And if it is not enabled, the other options do nothing: the main switch rules.

docs.title: Session and security options
docs.text:
In Setup → Setup → General setup there are several options that affect access:

  • Session timeout (secs): maximum session time; 9000 seconds by default.
  • Enable HTTPS access: forces HTTPS in the console.
  • Use SSL certificate and Path of SSL certificate: certificate and path; /etc/ssl/certs/pandoraitsm.pem by default.
  • Access port: access port, 80 by default.
  • Public access to server: public URL; it must include the /pandoraitsm suffix. If configured wrongly, the console can become unreachable.
  • API password: global password for API requests. API v2 tokens are per user; do not confuse them.
  • Login hash password: used to generate a unique pre-authentication URL.
  • Hide version: hides the version in the footer and on the login screen.
  • Show modal last time logged: shows the user the date and time of their last access.

If you enable HTTPS, check the certificate and the trust chain. PHP may need the CA file declared in openssl.cafile. An expired certificate does not warn in the documentation; the browser does.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check The super administrator cannot log in with AD/LDAP It is local by design Use the local password A remote user cannot log in and the password is correct Fallback disabled or remote bind failing Check the method and the Test LDAP/AD does not connect DNS, port, TLS or Base DN Run the Test and check the log The user is created without a profile or group Incomplete auto-creation Check level, profile, group and company The 2FA code is rejected Clock out of sync Sync the server time The superadmin 2FA reset link does not arrive SMTP down Check the mail configuration The console does not load after enabling HTTPS Wrong certificate or public URL Check Apache, the certificate and access_public The user is blocked Failed attempts Wait the configured minutes or check the user

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use a central directory if one exists; do not duplicate accounts.
  • Keep a local super administrator as a rescue path.
  • Choose least privilege in remote user auto-creation.
  • Force 2FA for administrators, not just warn them.
  • Review the password policy after every organisational change.
  • Check HTTPS and the public URL before saving.
  • Document which method each group uses and who can change it.
  • Test both remote and local access before considering the configuration closed.

docs.text:

  • Licensing and limits (1.4).
  • Email and notifications (Part 03).
  • API and tokens (Part 11).

docs.title: Companies and contacts
docs.text:
In Pandora ITSM, a company is not a decorative record in a list: it is a boundary. It changes what a user sees in the CRM, in the inventory and in some reports. It is not the only boundary, though: groups still rule tickets —except for the grouped-only-by-company type—, time, changes and the wiki. Confusing the two is the fastest way to build an ACL that looks broken while doing exactly what you asked for.

This chapter does not describe forms or fields. It explains what a company represents, how a contact differs from a user and in which sections the company decides something. The forms and their configuration live in Part 08.

docs.title: Company, group and user
docs.text:
Three pieces, three different jobs:

  • Company: the customer or organisation. It is assigned on the user record, in the Company field, and it is optional.
  • Group: the unit of visibility. A user can belong to several groups, and each group grants a different visibility.
  • User: the account that signs in to the console or receives email. Its group and profile combination decides what it can do.

A company is not a group. A user can belong to several groups but has only one company assigned. The group is the general permission axis; the company only matters in the sections that take it into account, and when it does, it matters a lot.

The four user types split the ground differently: the grouped user depends on its groups and profiles; the grouped-only-by-company user turns the company into an access limit for tickets; the standalone user sees its own tickets and its company; the super administrator bypasses the ACL. Types and profiles are covered in chapter 2.1.

docs.title: Contact versus user
docs.text:
A contact and a user may represent the same person, but they are not the same thing. One is a record in the commercial directory; the other is an account with access. The difference is not cosmetic: it changes who can open a ticket, who consumes a licence and who can modify whom.

Contact User What it is Person in the CRM directory Console account Where it is managed CRM → Company → Contacts People → User management Credentials None Yes, except email-only users Groups and profiles No Yes Company Belongs to a company May be assigned a company Licence Does not count May count if its profile grants an administrator bit What it is for Commercial email, campaigns, deals and contact lists Tickets, work units, projects and the rest of the console Who creates it A profile with CM UM or super administrator When the company is deleted Deleted in cascade Not deleted: its assignment must be reviewed

A contact does not sign in, has no permissions and does not open tickets. If you need someone to open tickets, create a user, even an email-only user. The contact tells you whom to call and whom to email a campaign to; the user operates the system.

The same person can exist twice, once as a user and once as a contact. There is no automatic synchronisation between the two records: if a phone number changes, someone must update it in both places. That duplication is convenient for the CRM and a small tax for whoever maintains the data.

Contacts belong to the CRM. In the current version, listing, creating or modifying them requires the CM permission; CR or CW is not enough. It is a conservative decision: the commercial directory is not exposed to anyone who can see companies.

When a company is deleted, its contacts disappear with it. Child companies do not: their parent company is left empty and they become roots. Users are not deleted either, but their assignment points to a company that no longer exists, so it is worth reviewing.

docs.title: The company in the ACLs
docs.text:
Companies form a tree. Each one may have a parent company and a manager, who owns it. Access is inherited downwards: if you have access to a company, you have access to its child companies. The standalone user is the exception and stays within its own company.

One detail surprises more than one reader: in the current code, the CM permission is not limited to the branch. A user with CM sees every company, not just those in its hierarchy. Parent-child inheritance applies to CR and CW; CM is the master key. If someone grants CM thinking "so they can manage their customer", they are handing over the whole portfolio. The super administrator, as usual, bypasses the ACL.

The other sections do not work the same way. This is the table worth keeping close:

Section What rules What the company does CRM: companies and contacts Company Main axis. Companies: CR lists, CW creates, CM edits and deletes. Contacts: CM. Deals Company Listed with CR; created, edited and deleted with CM, always within accessible companies. Invoices Company Only invoices from accessible companies are shown; invoice permissions are independent of CRM permissions. Inventory Profile and company Visibility includes the objects of the user's company, in addition to public, owned and assigned objects. Tickets Group, profile and company depending on the user type The general axis is group and profile. For the grouped-only-by-company type, the company does act as an ACL: it only sees tickets created by users of its company, within its groups. For the other types, the company is only a search filter. Projects Owner and members The company is a contractual link and a filter, not a permission. Reports Profile The company appears as a filter in some reports, not as a permission. Time, changes, wiki, downloads and knowledge base Group and profile The company plays no part.

The practical conclusion: the company does not replace the group. If you build the hierarchy and forget the profiles, you see nothing; if you hand out CM without looking, the hierarchy stops being useful.

docs.title: Practical cases
docs.text:
A matrix with customer companies. My Company is the root; Customer #A and Customer #B hang from it. A user with CR assigned to My Company sees its own company and both children. A user with CM sees every company in the system, even outside its branch. If the goal is for each manager to handle only its branch, stay with CR and CW and keep CM scarce.

The same person in two places. Ana is a customer's purchasing manager. As a contact, she receives campaigns and appears in deals; as a user, she opens tickets when something fails. They are two separate records, with different permissions and different lifecycles. If Ana leaves the company, deactivate her user and delete her contact: one does not drag the other along.

Moving a user to another company. Moving someone to another company changes what they see in the CRM and in the inventory. It does not change their tickets: those are governed by the group, unless the user is grouped only by company, where the company also narrows access. It does not change their profiles either; that requires editing their groups.

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Create the root company first and assign it to users before you start with customers, contacts and contracts.
  • Model the hierarchy according to who must see whom, not according to the sales org chart.
  • Keep contacts as a directory: do not use them as support accounts.
  • Grant CM sparingly and review who has it; its scope is the whole portfolio.
  • When you delete a company, review its child companies and the users that pointed to it.
  • For the remaining permissions, go back to chapter 2.1; for tickets and inventory, to chapters 3.1 and 4.1.

The company decides who the customer is; the group decides who can see it. When the two are confused, the ACL does what you ask, not what you want.

docs.title: Tickets and incidents
docs.text:
A ticket is the smallest unit of support work: someone has a problem, someone else takes ownership, and the system records what happened, when, and with how much effort. Everything else —emails, calls, messages— is a way of reaching the ticket, not a replacement for it.

The temptation to treat the mailbox as the support queue is strong and always ends the same way: requests without an owner, answers that exist only in one person's inbox, and statistics nobody dares to look at. Pandora ITSM exists so that every request has a number, a status and a responsible person.

docs.title: What a ticket is
docs.text:
A ticket can be an incident, a request, a question or a small change. What defines it is not the subject but the contract:

  • It has a creator who describes the problem.
  • It has an owner who commits to solving it.
  • It has a status that says where it stands.
  • It has a group that determines who can see and work on it.
  • It has a history of comments, files and time.

Without an owner, the ticket is a note in the air. Without a status, nobody knows whether the problem is still alive. Without a group, visibility becomes a lottery.

docs.title: Who is who
docs.text:
More people take part in a ticket than it seems. Confusing the roles is an endless source of arguments:

Role What it does Creator Finds the problem and describes it. Keeps visibility even if the ticket changes group. Owner Is responsible for solving it. It can be a user or a team, but only one at a time. Editor Enters the ticket into the system, even if they are neither its creator nor its solver. Contributor Provides information without being creator or owner. Associated user Has taken part at some point and receives notifications. Support team Groups several users and allows collaborative work or automatic distribution.

The Contacts tab shows the full list of participants and their role. Edit permissions allow you to create tickets; seeing someone else's ticket requires visibility over their group.

docs.title: How a ticket is created
docs.text:
Manual creation is still the standard: Support → Create new ticket. The form shows the common fields and the custom fields of the selected type.

In Setup → Setup → Issue setup → Ticket submission settings you can choose the creation mode:

  • Manual: all available fields. It is always accessible.
  • Simplified: only the mandatory fields: title, type, criticality, group, description, mandatory custom fields and files.
  • Smart: the user writes a question and the system searches the knowledge base before opening the ticket. If the answer solves the question, it can be marked as solved; if not, the ticket is created with the context. It needs an OpenAI API Key and a well-tuned System prompt.

Smart mode is not a fortune teller: if the knowledge base is empty or the prompt is too generic, it will return beautiful but useless answers. It is a way to avoid repeated tickets, not an excuse to stop documenting.

The message that opens the assistant is configured in Setup → Setup → Issue setup, in the Smart Ticketing Welcome message field. It accepts the __user_name__ (full name) and __user_id__ (user identifier) macros; if you leave the default value, the standard Pandora ITSM text is used.

Tickets can also be created by email. That path has its own rules and is explained in 3.4 Email and support.

docs.title: Teams and availability
docs.text:
A support team lets several people work on the same queue. It is created in People → Teams, needs the support bit enabled and is configured in Support → Teams.

Working modes:

  • Collaborative work: the ticket is assigned to the team and all its members can see and work on it.
  • Round Robin: rotating distribution among members.
  • Load Balanced: assignment to the member with the least active workload.
  • Availability: only assigns to users with an active status in the Timetracker.
  • Fallback: if nobody is available, the ticket goes to a specific user. If none is configured, it stays assigned to the team.

Automatic distribution is convenient until someone forgets to activate their shift. If the Timetracker does not reflect reality, the algorithm will hand tickets to people who have been offline for two hours. Automation does not fix poor availability management.

docs.title: Ticket anatomy
docs.text:
The main fields are title, description, criticality, group, type and status. The description supports rich HTML, links and images, and the ticket can carry attached files.

Advanced parameters contains the fields that are not always visible:

  • Parent ticket: parent-child relationship between tickets.
  • Project Task: link to a project task.
  • Change: link to a change.
  • Inventory objects: traceability of the affected elements.
  • Emails in copy: third parties who receive a copy without access to the application.

The Editor and Creator group are fixed for auditing: they cannot be changed and are used as filters in workflow rules.

docs.title: Work units
docs.text:
The conversation of a ticket is built with work units (WU). Each one can include:

  • Time dedicated (hours): time spent.
  • Private work unit: visible only to administrators and to its author.
  • Internal work unit: hidden from the ticket creator.
  • Add to project's cost: charges the cost to the project.
  • Work unit shared with: mentions another user, who receives a notice.
  • Description: rich text, links and images.

Every WU, file or status change generates notifications to the associated users. That is the difference between a living ticket and a document someone opened once. Mentions are written as @user in the WU description or in a comment; the mentioned user receives a notification and can open the ticket from the bell.

docs.title: Types and custom fields
docs.text:
In Support → Tickets types → View tickets types you define ticket types. Each type can have its own fields: single-line text, long text, date, numeric, true/false, Combo and Linked.

Details worth learning before they bite:

  • Global field creates a field common to all types.
  • Show in the list of tickets displays it in the list.
  • Required makes it mandatory.
  • In a mandatory Combo, the option string must start with a comma so the first option stays empty.
  • Linked fields chain a parent field to a child field. For example, Peripherals with Keyboard,Mouse and a second field showing Keyboard|USB, Keyboard|Bluetooth, Mouse|USB.

A ticket type with twenty mandatory fields does not improve information: it improves the speed at which the user abandons the form. Add fields when they will really be used in filters, reports or workflows.

docs.title: Ticket templates
docs.text:
Templates create repetitive tickets without copy and paste. They are managed in Support → Ticket Types → Templates and are associated with a ticket type.

The list shows Name, Description, Ticket type and the Edit, Duplicate and Delete actions. A template belongs to a single type, but a type can have several templates. To reuse a template in another type, duplicate it and adjust the fields.

Creating or editing a template asks for a name, description and ticket type; the full ticket form then appears, including advanced fields. Attachments are not part of the template.

When you create a ticket and the selected type has templates, a Select template selector appears below the title. The first template is selected by default; the None option keeps normal creation. Changing the type refreshes the selector with that type's templates and fills the fields with the stored values.

The template also works with the simplified form. Advanced fields included in the template are submitted and processed even if they are not shown in the interface; the simple form limits what is visible, not what is stored.

If a ticket type field is used by a template, it cannot be changed or deleted in a way that invalidates the template. External entities referenced by a template (a group, a user, an inventory object) are not validated on deletion: if they disappear, the template shows an empty field.

docs.title: Statistics and work orders
docs.text:
The ticket statistics tab summarises times, work units, activity by user, status, group, company and SLA. It is useful for answering concrete questions, not for decorating a meeting.

Work orders are created from templates in Support → Tickets types → Work order templates. Templates use macros such as _incident_id_, _incident_title_, _owner_, _author_, _status_, _resolution_, _time_used_ or custom fields. The work order is generated as a PDF and can be validated by uploading the version signed by the customer.

docs.title: Bulk operations and import
docs.text:
In Support → All tickets you can select several tickets and bulk-change status, priority, resolution, tag, group, owner or parent. The interface is shown to everyone, but every operation checks permissions. Bulk deletion exists; treat it as a demolition tool.

CSV import is in Support → Import tickets from csv. The column order is fixed: start, close, title, description, user, status, priority, group, update, creator, task, resolution, epilogue, parent, SLA disabled, SLA, type, score, copies, editor, creator group, last status, closed by, extra data, blocked, old statuses and resolutions, rating and comment. Custom fields go at the end, in the defined order, and must already exist.

The life cycle of these tickets is detailed in 3.2 Workflow and statuses; service metrics are in 3.3 SLA, escalation and quality.

docs.title: Workflow and statuses
docs.text:
A ticket status is the closest thing support has to a traffic light. While nobody touches it, the ticket looks alive; when everyone changes it at will, the traffic light becomes decoration. Pandora ITSM offers two mechanisms to make the flow meaningful: status mapping and workflow rules.

The first says where a ticket may go. The second decides what happens when it gets there. Using one without the other is like painting road signs on a road with no asphalt.

docs.title: Statuses are not labels
docs.text:
A ticket has a life cycle and several possible statuses. The main ones are:

Status What it means New The ticket has just been opened. The first-response SLA is measured here. Pending Customer The customer has the last word; their answer is expected. Pending Support Support has the last word; the response SLA keeps running. Re-opened A closed ticket becomes active again. For SLA purposes it behaves like support. Pending to be Closed It is solved, but confirmation or formal closure is pending. Pending on a third person It depends on a third party. Inactivity and response stop, although resolution time may keep running. Closed The ticket is closed. When it reaches this status, the epilogue appears.

The epilogue is not decoration: it explains what was done and why. A closed ticket without an epilogue is a ticket nobody will be able to reinterpret six months later.

docs.title: Status mapping
docs.text:
Status mapping is configured in Support → Workflow → Status mapping. It defines which statuses and resolutions are available at each point and forces the ticket through the phases the organisation considers necessary.

A simple example: a new ticket can only move to assigned; from there, to pending closure; and from there, to closed with resolution "solved" or "incomplete". If it is closed as incomplete, it can be reopened and sent back into the loop.

By default, any super administrator can change a ticket status —unless it is blocked— without respecting the mapping. It is a deliberate escape valve: if the flow is designed as a cage, someone will eventually open it with a hammer.

docs.title: Workflow rules
docs.text:
Rules are managed in Support → Workflow → Workflow rules and only super administrators can create or edit them. Each rule has a description and an execution mode:

  • Cron: evaluated on each cron run, usually every five minutes.
  • Real time: evaluated when a ticket is created or edited.

By default, only open tickets are checked. To include closed tickets, enable Check closed tickets when running workflow rules in Setup → Setup → Issue setup → Workflows.

Pandora ITSM ships with a set of sample rules disabled by default. You can modify and enable them, or create new ones from scratch. Before enabling someone else's rule, read its conditions: an inherited rule may do things that no longer make sense in your organisation.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Each rule can have one or more conditions. When creating them, you choose ticket fields and define how they combine:

  • Match all fields: all must be met.
  • Match any field: one is enough.
  • No match: met when there is no match.

Details that change the result:

  • Priority is numeric, and a higher priority does not include lower ones. If you filter by 3, you are not filtering by 1 and 2 as well.
  • When you choose a ticket type, its custom fields appear and can be used in the condition.
  • The default relationship between conditions in the same rule is OR: if one is met, the rule runs.
  • Conditions can be reordered; evaluation order matters when there are several actions.
  • The Tags condition is met when the ticket has at least one of the selected tags. Tags are created beforehand in Support → Tickets → Tags.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
When the conditions are met, the rule runs one or more actions:

  • Change priority.
  • Change owner.
  • Change group.
  • Change status.
  • Send an email.
  • Add a work unit.
  • Change the update date.
  • Change the resolution.
  • Run a command on the server or a custom script.
  • Block or unblock.
  • Change the type.
  • Add tags.

The most useful actions are usually the boring ones: assign the ticket to the right group, raise the priority when it has been idle too long, and notify the owner. The spectacular actions —running commands, changing types, blocking— should have a very short guest list.

Tags classify without creating a new type. The Add tags action adds one or more tags to the ticket; it does not replace the ones it already had. Combine it with the Tags condition to create rules such as "if the ticket arrives with the VIP tag, add High priority and notify the team". If a tag is deleted, existing relations stop showing it.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Actions accept macros that are replaced with ticket values:

Macro Value _access_url_ Direct URL to the ticket _author_ Ticket creator _companymanager_ Manager of the ticket's company _creation_timestamp_ Creation date and time _fullname_ Recipient's full name _id_group_ Group identifier _id_priority_ Priority identifier _id_resolution_ Resolution identifier _id_status_ Status identifier _incident_auth_email_ Creator's email _incident_closed_by_ User who closed the ticket _incident_epilog_ Ticket epilogue _incident_group_email_ Group email _incident_id_ Ticket identifier _incident_own_email_ Owner's email _incident_title_ Title _name_group_ Group name _name_priority_ Priority name _name_resolution_ Resolution name _name_status_ Status name _owner_ Owner _sitename_ Site name _type_tickets_ Ticket type _update_timestamp_ Last update _username_ Recipient's login name

Custom fields also work as macros with the format _field_name_. If the name has spaces or strange characters, the macro may become a surprise; consistent naming, please.

docs.title: Practical recipes
docs.text:
Three rules that usually pay for the effort:

  1. High priority, immediate notice: if priority is 5 and status is New, change the owner to the on-call team and send an email with _incident_id_, _incident_title_ and _access_url_.
  2. Silent customer: if status is Pending Customer and the last update is older than the configured days, send a reminder and, if appropriate, move to Pending to be Closed.
  3. Orderly closure: when moving to Closed, require resolution and epilogue, and send the satisfaction survey if the group has it enabled.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause The rule never runs Conditions too restrictive or rule disabled It runs on closed tickets it should not touch Closed-ticket check token enabled It changes status and nothing else happens The action is in another rule with different conditions The email arrives without data Wrong macro or empty field The flow gets stuck Status mapping too rigid and with no escape valve

The metrics that measure this flow are explained in 3.3 SLA, escalation and quality.

docs.title: SLA, escalation and quality control
docs.text: An SLA (service level agreement) is a promise with a clock. If the clock only runs when convenient, the promise becomes literature. Pandora ITSM measures four different times and compares them with the limits the organisation has defined; the rest is interpreting the numbers without fooling yourself.

docs.title: Where it is configured
docs.text:
SLAs are managed in Support → View SLA and assigned at group level. The ticket's group determines which SLA applies, although the default SLA can be changed during creation and the group SLA can be reloaded with the reload button.

The main fields:

Field What it measures First response SLA (in hours) Maximum time until the owner's first response. SLA Base Informative relationship with another SLA. SLA Type Normal, third party or both. Max. response time (in hours) Maximum time between the creator's last work unit and the next response. Max. resolution time (in hours) Maximum ticket lifetime until resolution. Max. tickets at the same time Maximum number of open tickets at once. Max. ticket inactivity (in hours) Maximum time without any update. Disable SLA on holidays Excludes holidays from the calculation.

SLA Type changes the set of tickets included in the calculation:

  • Normal: tickets that are neither closed nor pending on a third party.
  • Third party: only those pending on a third party.
  • Both: all tickets that are not closed. In this case, a specific inactivity limit can be configured for third parties.

docs.title: The four clocks
docs.text:
The ticket view and statistics show four metrics. All have the same structure: Used, Limit and Deviation.

Metric What it measures First response (FRT) From opening to the agent's first response. Response time Between later responses from the creator and the agent. For it to count correctly, the status must be Pending Support. Inactivity time Since the ticket's last update. Resolution (TTR) From creation to resolution.

Deviation is the part most often misunderstood: if what was used is less than the limit, the deviation is the time left over (positive); if it is greater, it is the delay. When the limit is exceeded, the SLA alert fires.

docs.title: Time windows and holidays
docs.text:
An SLA does not have to count twenty-four hours a day. Scheduled defines the windows in which it is counted, with a simple or detailed mode. The detailed mode can adjust by minutes, but requires cron to run at that granularity. If cron runs every five minutes, promising minute-level precision is a creative way to lie.

Disable SLA on holidays excludes holidays. Holidays are defined in Setup → Setup → Issue setup → Customization → Special day, where you can also indicate whether they are working days.

docs.title: What "the SLA will breach" means
docs.text:
It means the system will send an email to the ticket owner warning that one of the criteria of the associated SLA has been breached. The SLA applies by group, so a ticket can inherit a different SLA when it changes group.

The ticket list can be filtered by breached or non-breached SLA, and the ticket view shows a histogram with met and unmet periods, plus a compliance percentage by date range. Those metrics are also available through the API and support reports.

docs.title: Escalation
docs.text:
Escalating is not "pass the ticket to someone else and forget about it". A healthy escalation changes at least one of these three things:

  • Owner: from one person to another or to a team.
  • Group: from first level to second level, or to a specialised team.
  • Priority: because the real impact has changed.

Workflow rules are how you automate those changes: reassign to the on-call team, raise the priority when the ticket has been in Pending Support for too long, or notify the manager when a threshold is crossed. Manual escalation is still needed for what no form anticipated.

docs.title: Quality control
docs.text:
Quality assurance (Q/A) and feedback are configured at two levels:

  • General: Setup → Setup → Issue setup → Ticket behavior → Disable ticket score disables rating.
  • Per group: People → Groups management → Send customer satisfaction email decides whether the survey is sent on closure.

By default, when a ticket is closed the creator is asked how it was resolved. The rating can only be good or bad, with optional text. It is associated with the ticket and its owner, and only users with Q/A permissions and the creator can see it.

If the rating is negative and Survey Questions is enabled, a survey with the configured options is shown. It can only be answered once. A survey that arrives late, or asks the same thing as the ticket, does not improve quality: it only generates more email.

docs.title: Creation limits
docs.text:
In People → Groups management you can limit tickets per group and user:

  • Total ticket limit: maximum total tickets, open or closed.
  • Open ticket limit: maximum open tickets at the same time.

The limit can be forced (no more tickets allowed) or only warn. A value of 0 means no limit. The calculation counts tickets from the last year from the current date, not the entire history of humanity.

docs.title: Email and support
docs.text:
Email is the easiest front door for users and the easiest one for administrators to break. In Pandora ITSM it is not enough to configure an SMTP server: you have to decide which mailboxes are read, which senders are accepted, and what happens when a message does not fit any queue.

The golden rule is simple: if an email does not match a group queue, it is not processed. There is no rescue inbox or apology message. It stays wherever it is, waiting for someone to read it by hand.

The resulting ticket follows the rules of 3.1 Tickets and incidents and 3.2 Workflow and statuses.

docs.title: Two addresses that are not the same
docs.text:
Each group's email configuration has two fields that are often confused:

  • Email destination: addresses or aliases of the mailbox Pandora ITSM reads to create or update tickets. It accepts several addresses and regular expressions, one per line.
  • Email origin: filter of valid senders. Only emails that match this field are accepted for creating or updating tickets. It also accepts several addresses and regular expressions.

The first says "which mailbox we are talking about"; the second says "who is allowed to write to it". If Email origin is empty, any sender is accepted. Mix them up and you will end up with tickets created by anyone or legitimate emails ignored.

docs.title: Email configuration
docs.text: The general configuration is in Setup → Setup → Email. There are two halves:

docs.title: Sending (SMTP)
docs.text:
• System mail from address: sender of notifications.
  • Encryption: none, SSL/TLS, SSLv2, SSLv3, STARTTLS or Microsoft OAuth 2.0.
  • SMTP Host, SMTP Port, SMTP User and SMTP Password.
  • User ID, Client ID, Tenant ID and Secret for OAuth.
  • SMTP Queue retries, Max pending mail and Max. emails sent per execution to control the queue.

The Test button checks the connection. A "successful test" only proves the server answers; it does not prove the email reaches the destination inbox.

docs.title: Receiving (POP/IMAP)
docs.text:
• Encryption, POP/IMAP Host, POP/IMAP Port, POP/IMAP User and POP/IMAP Password.
  • User ID, Client ID, Tenant ID and Secret for OAuth.
  • Select IMAP or POP: IMAP is usually the sensible choice; POP tends to move or delete messages and complicates traceability.
  • Message delimiter: marks where to cut the reply thread.
  • Compatibility: Gmail, Microsoft 365, Outlook, Dreamhost or others.

If the server requires OAuth, you must connect the application and renew the secret when it expires. An expired secret does not send a polite email: it simply stops receiving.

docs.title: Group email queue
docs.text:
The group configuration defines what happens to messages arriving in its queue:

  • Email destination and Email origin.
  • Autocreate users: creates the user if the sender does not exist.
  • Grant access to users: gives them access to the application.
  • Send welcome email and Welcome email: welcome message, with the _password_ macro if the password is sent.
  • Default status, User type, Default company, Default user's profile and Default ticket type.

Combining Autocreate users and Grant access to users is convenient and dangerous at the same time: anyone who writes to the mailbox can become a user. Enable it only if the origin filter and the network perimeter justify it.

docs.title: What happens when an email arrives
docs.text:
1. Pandora ITSM reads the configured mailbox.
  2. It looks for a group queue whose Email destination matches the destination address.
  3. It checks that the sender matches Email origin.
  4. If there is no match, the email is not processed.
  5. If there is a match, it looks for an existing ticket by subject or headers.
  6. If none exists, it creates a new ticket.
  7. If one exists, it adds a work unit, updates the ticket and records the email body as a comment.

On creation, the ticket takes these values:

  • Creator: user associated with the from address, if it exists or if autocreation is enabled.
  • Editor: the same from user.
  • Group: the queue's group.
  • Owner: the group's default user, if defined.
  • Title: the subject.
  • Description: the body.
  • Notifications: TO and CC addresses other than the queue address.
  • Attachments: the message files.

docs.title: Updating a ticket by email
docs.text:
Some fields can be changed with a text block in the message body:

[INCIDENT]
GROUP: Support
ASSIGNED_TO: operator
PRIORITY: 3
STATUS: Assigned
RESOLUTION: Invalid
[INCIDENT]

Supported fields:

Field Value GROUP Group name. ASSIGNED_TO Owner's login name. PRIORITY Number from 0 (lowest) to 5 (highest). STATUS Status name. RESOLUTION Resolution name.

If the syntax is not exact, the changes are not applied and the text ends up as a comment. Pandora ITSM does not guess intentions; if you meant to change the status and wrote STATUS : Assigned, you will get a lovely comment and an unchanged ticket.

The time of a work unit can also be adjusted:

[WORKUNIT]
TIME_USED: 0.05
[WORKUNIT]

If not specified, 0.25 hours are used. Again: syntax rules.

docs.title: Masking addresses
docs.text: When someone replies "to all", the email body may carry other people's addresses. In Setup → Setup → Issue setup → Email sending options → Masking email addresses they can be replaced with the wildcard xxxx@xxxx.xxxx. It is useful to avoid leaking contacts into the ticket history, although it is no substitute for a decent data policy.

docs.title: Microsoft 365 and OAuth
docs.text:
For Microsoft 365, register an application in Azure AD:

  1. Go to the Azure portal and search for Azure Active Directory.
  2. App registrations → New registration.
  3. Choose a name, account type and a Web Redirect URI, for example http://localhost/pandora.
  4. Copy Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID.
  5. Create a Client Secret in Certificates & secrets and copy it immediately: it is shown only once.
  6. Add the valid redirect URLs in Authentication → Add a platform → Web.
  7. If a non-administrator user is used, review API permissions and user consent in Azure AD.

Then enter Client ID, Tenant ID and Secret in the SMTP and/or POP/IMAP configuration of Pandora ITSM. If permissions change, generate a new secret. Secrets expire; so do the emails that depend on them.

The detailed procedure, including non-administrator user consent, is in A4 Microsoft 365 integration.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Emails do not create tickets Destination address does not match any queue The email arrives but is ignored Sender does not match Email origin The ticket is created without an owner The group has no default user The user does not exist Autocreation disabled or user in the blacklist Email changes are not applied Wrong [INCIDENT] syntax Replies are cut incorrectly Message delimiter misconfigured Microsoft 365 stops working Expired OAuth secret Large attachments fail Email or mail server size limit

docs.title: Knowledge base
docs.text:
A knowledge base is the support team's memory. Its goal is not to accumulate articles, but to prevent the same problem from being solved from scratch twice. When a ticket is closed and the solution is not documented, the knowledge leaves with the person who solved it.

Pandora ITSM organises that memory into articles that belong to a category and, optionally, to a product type. Access can be refined by group, so each group sees only what it should.

The 3.6 Wiki covers internal procedures; the knowledge base focuses on recurring solutions.

docs.title: Where it is
docs.text:
The main view is Support → Knowledge base → Browse. It shows a filter and a summary by category. If a category has more than six articles, a link lists them all.

Each article opens by clicking its name. If the user is a super administrator or has KW or KM permissions in an assigned profile, they can create, edit and delete articles. Other users can only read.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
In Support → Knowledge base → Categories you classify articles. The list shows the icon, name, parent category, description, number of articles and the delete option. To edit, click the name; creation uses the same interface.

A useful category hierarchy is usually shallow. If reaching an article requires crossing five levels, users will search Google before the knowledge base.

docs.title: Product types
docs.text:
In Support → Knowledge base → Product types you narrow the classification further. Each product has an identifier, icon, name, description and number of articles. It can be edited by clicking the name and deleted from each row.

The difference between category and product is the difference between "how it is solved" and "what it affects". An article can be in the "Networks" category and the "Perimeter firewall" product. If that distinction is not used, you end up with a category called "Misc" that contains the universe.

docs.title: Access management
docs.text:
The knowledge base is accessible to users with permissions in their profile, but visibility can be refined by product type and group in Support → Knowledge base → Manage access → Create.

Select a product type and a group. Access management requires the KM permission. Created relationships cannot be edited: they can only be deleted. It is a design decision that forces you to think before saving, although it also invites duplicates when someone makes a mistake.

docs.title: Creating articles
docs.text:
There are two paths:

  1. From the list: create a new article and fill in title, category, product, language, body and attachments.
  2. From a closed ticket: when the status changes to Closed, Pandora ITSM offers to add the ticket content to the knowledge base. Choosing the add-to-knowledge-base option opens the form with the ticket data preloaded.

The second path is the most valuable: the solution is already written, with its context and its tests. You only need to edit it so it makes sense outside the ticket.

A good article is not a transcript of the ticket. It should include:

  • The symptom, in the words someone searching would use.
  • The context or likely cause.
  • The diagnostic steps.
  • The solution.
  • Limitations or cases where it does not apply.
  • Links to other articles or procedures.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write the title as a question or symptom, not as a ticket number.
  • Use categories and products consistently.
  • Review old articles when the product changes.
  • Link the article from the ticket that originated it.
  • Do not store credentials, tokens or personal data in the knowledge base.
  • If an article needs five screenshots to explain one click, the procedure can probably be simplified.

docs.title: Wiki
docs.text:
The internal wiki is the team's shared notebook: procedures, runbooks, minutes, links and that explanation someone wrote once and everyone consults every month. It is not an incident knowledge base, even if it looks like one; the knowledge base answers "how is this problem solved", the wiki answers "how does this work internally".

Pandora ITSM includes a simple wiki with permissions by profile and by page. That simplicity is a virtue: it does not try to be Confluence, but it does not force you to set up a separate server to document day-to-day work either.

The 3.5 Knowledge base is meant for incident solutions; the wiki is for procedures and internal documentation.

docs.title: Read and write permissions
docs.text:
General access is controlled by profile bits:

  • WR: read permission.
  • WW: write permission.
  • WM: wiki administration, including access lists.
  • Super administrator: can do everything, as in the rest of the product.

There is also an extended ACL per page. In Wiki → Wiki, inside each page, Read ACL and Write ACL decide which users can read or edit it.

The most frequently forgotten rule: if the ACL list is empty, the page is accessible to everyone. When a user is added, only that user —and wiki administrators— have access. An empty ACL does not mean "nobody"; it means "everybody".

Other particularities:

  • A user can be added to an ACL without having the profile's WR/WW permissions; in that case the ACL is useless to them.
  • A user can appear several times in a list; to exclude them, delete every occurrence.
  • Pandora ITSM does not warn when an ACL locks someone out. Documentation is no substitute for testing with the real user.

docs.title: Wiki menu
docs.text:
In Wiki → Admin pages you manage pages, including the special side_menu page that defines the side menu.

To add a link to an internal page, use the page name and a URL such as:

index.php?sec=wiki&sec2=operation/wiki/wiki&page=Office

For an external link, the URL must include http:// or https://. The link opens in the same window, so warn anyone using it: leaving the console by accident is a deeply rooted tradition.

Menu links can be deleted from Admin pages. After saving, re-enter to see the changes. If they do not appear, it is not black magic: it is menu cache.

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: The full syntax is in Wiki → Syntax. The essentials:

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
!Heading H2
!!Heading H3
!!!Heading H4
!!!!Heading H5

The more exclamation marks, the lower the level. They must be at the start of the line. After saving, each heading has a button to edit only that section.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
* Fruit
** Apple
*** Granny smith
** Orange
* Vegetables

Numbered lists use #, ##, ### with the same logic.

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
'''bold'''
''italic''
'__underlined__'
'--strikethrough--'

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
[Sample page|sample subpage]
[External page|https://www.example.com/]
[http://www.example.com/]

Relative links must start with ./; otherwise they are interpreted as internal wiki pages.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Internal images are uploaded in Wiki → Upload and referenced like this:

[./wiki_data/upload/image_name.png]
[./wiki_data/upload/dir1/image_name.png]

External images can also be linked, although hosting them on the server is better. Useful options:

[http://example.com/image.jpg|link=http://example.com/|center|title=Example image]

docs.title: Table of contents, code and formatting
docs.text:
• {TOC} generates a table of contents from the headings.
  • {{ ... }} shows code without formatting.
  • ---- inserts a horizontal line.
  • ^ escapes special characters.
  • {html}...{/html} inserts raw HTML. A heading inserted this way will not have a section edit button.
  • {br} inserts a line break.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use the wiki for stable procedures, not for a ticket's day-to-day work.
  • Define an index page and a side menu with the important pages.
  • Assign an owner to each page and review it when the product changes.
  • Do not paste passwords, tokens or personal data.
  • If a page needs ten subpages to explain a procedure, the procedure may need simplifying.
  • Test ACLs with an unprivileged user before trusting them.

docs.title: Downloads and directories
docs.text:
Pandora ITSM can distribute files to customers and users without resorting to an FTP server, a WeTransfer link or an email with a 40 MB attachment. The downloads section organises material into folders, classifies it by category and decides which groups can see it.

It is tempting to use this section as a junk drawer. Remember that everything published here has an audience: if you do not know who should download it, you are not ready to upload it.

docs.title: Folders
docs.text:
Files are grouped into logical folders in Support → Downloads → Folders. From there, new folders are created with Create.

The folder is logical, not physical: all files are stored in:

/var/www/html/pandoraitsm/attachment/downloads/

That is why file names must be unique, even across different folders. If two people upload manual.pdf, the second will overwrite or collide with the first. The upload dialog lets you rename the file before saving.

There is a special folder called Others for files uploaded without a folder. If it appears, someone has ignored the form. Files can be edited to assign a folder; when no orphans remain, the folder disappears.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text: In Support → Downloads → Categories you create categories. Each has a name and an optional icon. The category is what is later linked to groups to control access, so it is not a cosmetic detail.

docs.title: Uploading files
docs.text:
In Support → Downloads → List you see folders, their last update and the number of files. The Upload file button opens the form to select one or more files and assign a category and folder.

Options for each file:

  • Private work unit: only administrators see it.
  • Internal: invisible to the ticket creator and to copied addresses.
  • Description: text that helps identify what is being downloaded.

The default maximum size is 50 MB per file, although the real limit depends on PHP and web server configuration. If the file exceeds the limit, the error may appear before Pandora ITSM even sees it.

Deleting files is irreversible. There is no recycle bin. Before deleting several, check that they are not the only copy of something important.

docs.title: Access management
docs.text:
In Support → Downloads → Access you link categories to groups. An item belongs to a category, and the category has one or more groups with access. That is how you control which users can download what.

To create a relationship, choose a category and a group and save. The interface allows saving with the default "no category and any group", so review the selection before confirming. An overly broad access does not raise an error; it simply exposes material to people who should not see it.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use descriptive, unique file names.
  • Always assign a category and a folder; avoid Others.
  • Review group access before publishing.
  • Do not upload material with personal data or credentials.
  • Document the version or date in the file name.
  • Delete carefully: there is no undo.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Pandora ITSM's inventory does not fail because of the console: it fails because of the data model. A list of devices can be put together in ten minutes; a useful inventory requires deciding beforehand which object types exist, which fields are shared, who can see what and how objects relate to each other. The rest —views, filters and widgets— comes almost for free.

This chapter covers the whole inventory: object types, custom and external fields, objects, hierarchy, stock, statuses, tags, ACL, CSV import and remote inventory from Pandora FMS. The Pandora FMS integration is detailed in chapter 11.4; here we explain what the inventory does with it.

The inventory tells you which objects the organisation has, where they are, who uses them and which contracts, tickets and changes they relate to. It does not discover the network on its own. Objects come in by hand, by CSV or from the Pandora FMS synchronisation.

docs.title: Object types
docs.text:
An object type defines the data template for a set of objects. A Computer does not have the same fields as a licence or a contract. The menu is Inventory → Object Types.

To create a type, click Create, fill in its characteristics and click Create again. To edit it, click its name. The list lets you duplicate a type with all its custom fields through Duplicate.

The type parameters are:

Parameter What it is for Name Object type name. Icon Associated icon; images are uploaded to images/objects/. Show in tree view If enabled, the type appears as a root in the tree view. Min. stock Minimum stock for the type. Max. stock Maximum stock for the type. Catalogs to show in overview Catalogs shown as sections in the object overview. Description Type description. Sync interval How often it synchronises with Pandora FMS: Never, Weekly, Every 15 days, Monthly or First time only.

Sync interval only appears when Pandora FMS nodes are configured and the type is associated with a Pandora FMS schema. Without the integration, there is nothing to synchronise.

docs.title: Custom and global fields
docs.text:
Each type has its own fields. They are managed from Actions → Fields in the type list: create them with Create, edit them by clicking their name and order them with the arrows in the actions column. Deletion lives there too.

Global fields are the useful exception: they are defined once in Inventory → Object types → Global Fields and added to every type. Each type can hide them or change their order, but the field is the same. Use them for what is always present: serial number, location, purchase date.

The properties shared by all fields are:

Property Effect Unique Only one object can hold that value; it works as an identifier. Inherit The object inherits owner, users and companies from its parent object. Show in list The field appears by default in the general list and can be used as a column. Prevent updates The field is not updated when remote inventory data arrives.

The available data types are: numeric, checkbox, text, option list, external field, date, web link, password and value with unit. In the option list, values are separated by commas in Combo values.

docs.title: External fields
docs.text:
An external field reads information from an additional database table, created by hand with the DB Manager. It is the way to link the inventory to your own catalogues without turning every value into a static list.

In a simple field you set two mandatory values: External table name, the exact table name, and Field to be displayed, the column shown. Objects update themselves when the table changes. Primary key, Foreign key and Parent table name are left empty: they belong to composite fields.

A composite field chains two tables. The parent table has a primary key; the child table has a foreign key pointing to it. When creating the parent field you set the Primary key; when creating the child, the Foreign key and the Parent table name. The result is a drop-down that depends on the previous value: if you clear the parent, the child can be chosen again.

The classic case is country and city. Create the tables with the DB Manager:

CREATE TABLE t_country (
    id_country INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE t_city (
    id_city INT,
    name TEXT,
    id_country INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (id_country) REFERENCES t_country(id_country)
);

Add the values with INSERT, create the Country field on t_country and the City field on t_city with id_city as the primary key, id_country as the foreign key and t_country as the parent table. From then on, any object of the chosen type can select a country and a city. If the field has Show in list, it also appears as a column and as a filter.

docs.title: Inventory objects
docs.text:
Objects are created in Inventory → Lists with Create. Before filling in fields, decide who can see them:

  • Owner: owner of the object.
  • Associated companies: associated companies.
  • Associated users: associated users.
  • Public: if enabled, everyone sees it.

Those four fields are the object's ACL. An object is visible to its owner, to associated users, to users of associated companies and to everyone if it is public. Nobody else sees it.

An object can have a Parent, which creates a hierarchy, and relationships with other objects. It also stores the type, status, contract, receipt date, issue date, EOL date, an image and a QR code.

The object view has two columns. On the right are the main data and actions; on the left, the tabs:

  • Custom fields.
  • Tickets: history of associated tickets.
  • Changes: associated changes.
  • Relationships.
  • Tracker: history of changes to the object and its children.
  • Associated users.

Objects of type Computer add Hardware, Software and Extended Info with the information collected from Pandora FMS.

Objects can be duplicated from the list with Duplicate; it is the quick way to register ten devices that only differ in the serial number. They can also be reclassified into another type: the system asks how each source field maps to the destination, converts internal identifiers and lets you fill in the new fields by hand. Some fields are discarded; review the result.

docs.title: Views, searches and bulk operations
docs.text:
Inventory → Lists offers four ways of looking at the same thing:

  • Overview: landing page with the inventory status and the main types.
  • List: data table with filters, configurable columns and export.
  • Tree: parent-child hierarchy, grouped by type.
  • Stock: stock control, explained below.

The search filters by free text —description, identifier and custom fields—, by status, by object type and by page size. The result can be exported to CSV.

In list mode you can select several objects and run bulk operations: delete, change the object type, parent, company, contract, owner or status. Deletion is irreversible; the rest can be undone object by object.

docs.title: Stock control
docs.text:
Stock is not kept as a loose number: it is calculated from two pieces. Each type has min_stock and max_stock; each object has a relationship limit (relation_limit, labelled Max relations in the interface).

  • With 0 or empty, the object counts as one unit and allows unlimited relationships.
  • With 1 or more, the object allows at most that number of relationships and appears on the second level of stock control.

The stock view has two levels. The first shows each type with its minimum, maximum and used stock, a percentage bar and actions to view objects, create a ticket, create a change or schedule a task. The second shows objects with a relationship limit and their usage percentage. If the total drops below the minimum, the warning turns red.

docs.title: Statuses and tags
docs.text:
Inventory → Status manages object statuses. Pandora ITSM ships five internal statuses: New, In use, Unused, Issued and Missing. They can be edited, and you can add your own. If a status that was assigned is deleted, the affected objects go back to New.

Tags (Inventory → Tags) work as in the rest of the console: name, colour and relationship with objects. They are not shown by default in the list; add them as a column or filter by them.

docs.title: Inventory ACL
docs.text:
Inventory has its own set of permissions:

Bit What it allows VR View the objects you have access to. VW Create, edit and delete objects; includes read access. VM Manage the whole inventory: objects, types, statuses, tags and catalogues.

Read access is not global: the object's visibility applies (public, owner, associated user or associated company). Writing requires VW or VM, and managing types, statuses and tags requires VM. The super administrator bypasses the ACL. The role of the company in the other sections is explained in chapter 2.3.

docs.title: Dashboards and widgets
docs.text:
The inventory provides its own dashboard widgets:

  • Inventory by status: percentage by status, filterable by type.
  • Inventory by object type: percentage by type, with multi-selection.
  • Top N stock inventory: the types with the highest usage percentage.
  • Stock relations: global stock and stock per object with a relationship limit.
  • Inventory counter: object count.
  • Inventory type boxes: shortcuts by object type.

docs.title: Importing from CSV
docs.text:
Bulk import lives in Inventory → Import CSV. Choose the object type, check the separator —| by default— and download the template with Download sample CSV. The template changes with the type because it includes its custom fields.

The file must have a header in the first row and at least nine columns in this order:

Position Column Content 1 Name Object name. Mandatory. 2 Owner Owner user. Mandatory and must exist. 3 Status Status by label or identifier. Mandatory. 4 Receipt date Receipt date. 5 Removal date Issue date. 6 Description Description. 7 Companies Company identifiers separated by commas. 8 Associated user User identifiers separated by commas. 9 Parent Identifier of the parent object, if any. 10+ Custom fields In the order of the type template.

Companies and users accept brackets and spaces, but a comma-separated list is the safe option. Custom fields are validated according to their type: numbers, closed lists, dates, external fields and uniqueness. If a row fails, the import reports the line and the reason.

This format is not what earlier versions of the documentation described: those listed manufacturer, contract, object type or public columns. In the current version the type is chosen in the form and the rest comes from the template. The code is the reference.

docs.title: Remote inventory from Pandora FMS
docs.text:
Remote inventory does not receive XML files from EndPoints directly: it synchronises from Pandora FMS. The Pandora FMS server collects the information with its EndPoints and Pandora ITSM reads it through the configured node, creating or updating the objects. Sending inventory directly from an EndPoint to Pandora ITSM no longer exists.

The destination configuration is in Setup → Pandora FMS Inventory, section Remote Inventory:

  • Default owner: owner of the new objects. It is mandatory.
  • Associated companies: default companies.
  • Associated users: default users.

Those values fill the objects created by the synchronisation and therefore decide their visibility. The Pandora FMS node, its credentials and its scope are configured in the integration; chapter 11.4 covers the full procedure.

Synchronisation is not immediate: each object type sets its pace with Sync interval (Never, Weekly, Every 15 days, Monthly or First time only). The type must be associated with the Pandora FMS schema for the option to appear.

The inventory cron is what makes this work. It runs include/inventory_cron.php and must be in crontab, usually every five minutes:

php /var/www/html/pandoraitsm/include/inventory_cron.php

On each run it records the inventory_crontask mark, synchronises the inventory from the Pandora FMS nodes respecting each type's interval, expires overdue schedules and removes Missing objects that no longer have a parent.

EndPoints are installed and configured in Pandora FMS, not in Pandora ITSM: they feed the monitoring server. ITSM only consumes the result through the node. Hardware, software and extended information for Computer objects arrive that way and are linked through id_pandora.

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Define few object types and fields with judgement; every extra field is paid for on every registration, filter and import.
  • Use global fields for what all types share and own fields for what is specific.
  • Model the hierarchy before importing: changing parents later is more expensive.
  • Review Min. stock and Max. relations before stock starts lying to you.
  • Respect the ACL from the start: owner, companies, users and Public decide who sees the object.
  • Do not turn the inventory into network discovery: if the data is not in Pandora FMS or the CSV, it does not appear.

docs.title: Change management
docs.text:
A change without a process is a bet. Sometimes it works and nobody asks; when it goes wrong, nobody knows who approved it, what was touched or why. Change management exists so that question has an answer before it is needed.

In Pandora ITSM, a change is not a ticket under another name. It has its own circuit: it is requested, authorised, planned with tasks, executed with work units and tickets, reviewed and closed. Every step leaves a trace in the Tracker, and the change team decides who can do what.

The entry point is Changes → Changes list. This chapter explains the full circuit, the configuration behind it and the ACL that protects it.

docs.title: Change types and roles
docs.text:
Pandora ITSM provides three change types:

  • Standard (pre-authorized): pre-authorised, low-risk changes such as restarting a server. When created, they are already authorised.
  • Emergency: critical changes that cannot wait, such as applying a security patch.
  • Normal: planned changes that require approval, such as a software update.

All three types are internal: they can be renamed, but not created or deleted from the interface.

Roles are not complete profiles, but parts within the change:

  • Initiator: the person who proposes the change.
  • Change manager: the person who supervises the impact and authorises or denies it. In practice this is usually the manager of the assigned team.
  • Change team: the group that executes the approved tasks.

The change manager and the team manager are separate fields. They may be the same person, but it is not mandatory; decide it before assigning changes.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
There are six change statuses and the system moves through most of them on its own:

Status What it means How it is reached New Request open, pending authorisation. When the change is created. Authorized Approved, still without tasks. On authorisation, or when a Standard change is created. Scheduled Scheduled, with pending tasks. When the first task is created. Implement In execution. When the first work unit is recorded. Review All tasks finished, pending validation. When all tasks are completed or verified. Closed Change closed. On validation, or on denial.

Denial has no way back: it closes the change immediately. Final validation cannot be undone either. The other transitions can be corrected by going back in the tasks, and the system returns the change to Implement if a task stops being finished.

docs.title: Requesting a change
docs.text:
Creation is in Changes → Changes list → Create. Before creating the first change there must be at least one change team; without one, the form has nobody to assign the work to. The first team created is assigned by default, so check the Team field on every creation.

The creation fields are:

  • Name: mandatory.
  • Template: change template, if any.
  • Status: disabled; the change is born in New.
  • Team: mandatory.
  • Type: Standard, Emergency or Normal.
  • Priority, Risk and Impact: change classification.
  • Manager: mandatory.

If the type is Standard (pre-authorized), the change goes directly to Authorized and the authorisation is recorded without the manager's intervention.

A newly created change shows the status line, the main data and the work tabs:

  • Authorization: approve or deny.
  • Notes: follow-up notes, which do not count as time.
  • Scheduled: change tasks.
  • Inventory objects: affected objects.
  • Associated tickets: tickets linked to the tasks.
  • Tracker: history of what happened.
  • Attachments: attached files.
  • Closure information: closure information, when the time comes.

Inventory objects are added from their tab and make clear which elements are affected. Attachments and notes follow the same logic: they document the change, but they do not replace the tasks. A note does not count as work; a work unit does.

docs.title: Approving and planning
docs.text:
Authorisation lives in the Authorization tab. The change manager can approve with a short assessment or deny. Denying closes the change at that very moment, without going through planning.

On approval, the change stays in Authorized. Planning starts when the first task is created and the change moves to Scheduled.

Each task has a name, manager, team, start and end date, estimated hours, optional parent task, description, priority, risk and impact. Child tasks are shown nested under the parent, which lets you break a large change down without losing the structure.

Tasks do not execute work on their own: they rely on tickets. A ticket is linked from its advanced options by choosing the change and the task. From then on it appears in Associated tickets, and the hours recorded on the ticket add to the task time.

docs.title: Implementing, reviewing and closing
docs.text:
During implementation, the team records work units on tasks and on associated tickets. Task progress is calculated from estimated and recorded time; when the manager marks it as Completed, the change moves forward.

The flow is:

  1. Tasks move from Pending to In process and then to Completed.
  2. When all are completed or verified, the change moves to Review.
  3. The change manager verifies each task (Verified).
  4. With all tasks verified, the change can be validated and closed.

Final validation is irreversible. If something does not add up, the change is denied and closed; if it is validated, it is closed with the epilogue written by the manager. The Closed status is also reached when the change is denied during authorisation.

docs.title: Change templates
docs.text:
Templates live in Changes → Management → Templates. A change team is required before creating one.

A template fills in the usual values of a change: type, status, team, priority, risk, impact and manager. It does not copy the name or description. When creating a change, choose the template and adjust what is needed; the template saves typing, it does not prevent changes.

docs.title: Statuses and types
docs.text:
Changes → Management → Statuses lets you rename statuses without changing their application order. The six statuses are those of the lifecycle: New, Authorized, Scheduled, Implement, Review and Closed. The order matters because the automatic transitions depend on it.

Changes → Management → Types lets you rename the three types. The Standard type remains the pre-authorised one; renaming it does not change the behaviour. That type is meant to be used from a pre-authorised template, not to disguise a normal change.

docs.title: Priorities, risks and impacts
docs.text:
There are three default values for each: low, medium and high, each with its colour. They are edited in Changes → Management → Priorities, Risks and Impacts.

They do not change the flow or authorise anything: they classify and allow filtering. A Normal change with high priority still needs approval; the colour does not replace it.

docs.title: Task statuses
docs.text:
Changes → Management → Tasks Statuses manages task statuses. The four internal ones are:

  • Pending: the task has not started.
  • In process: it is underway.
  • Completed: it has finished.
  • Verified: the manager confirms it is properly done.

Intermediate statuses can be added, always placed between Completed and Verified. Until all tasks are in Verified, the change cannot be validated and closed.

docs.title: Change teams
docs.text:
Teams are created in People → Teams and listed in Changes → Teams. For them to appear in the changes module, the Change option must be enabled on the team.

Each team has a manager, an email and a list of users. The email is used for team notifications; the manager is the fixed user and is added automatically. The other users are managed with Add users.

Deleting a team is dangerous: the changes planned with that team and all their tasks are deleted in cascade, with no way back. The interface asks you to type DELETE to confirm.

docs.title: Notifications and email templates
docs.text:
Setup → Setup → Changes setup decides which notifications are sent. Each one can be enabled or disabled:

  • Change created, updated and closed.
  • Task created, updated and closed.
  • Change status updated and task status updated.
  • Change work unit created and change task work unit created.
  • Task starts today: the task starts today.
  • Task ends today: the task ends today.

The start and end notices are sent once a day by cron to the people involved in the change and skip tasks that have already been verified. They are delivered through the channel configured in the user's profile (email, notification or both) and use the Change task starts today and Change task ends today templates.

The texts are edited in Setup → Email template setup, filtering by change templates. There you will find the subjects and bodies used by those notifications.

docs.title: Change ACL
docs.text:
The section uses three bits:
